title: Doubles, Bunny Chow, and Idli Shrimp: Drāvida Maps the Diaspora's Forgotten Food Routes
excerpt: Chef Aarthi Sampath's new East Village restaurant doesn't just serve Indian food — it traces how Indian flavours migrated across the Caribbean, Africa, and Southeast Asia.
body:
There is a dish in Trinidad called Doubles. It is two pieces of bara — soft, fried flatbread — filled with curried chickpeas, tamarind sauce, and a ferocious pepper sauce. It is eaten at street stalls at dawn. It costs a few dollars. And it is, by any reasonable accounting, Indian food — invented by the descendants of indentured labourers who left Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh for the Caribbean in the 19th century.

Most Indian restaurants in America would not know what to do with it. Chef Aarthi Sampath's Drāvida, which opened this month in Manhattan's East Village, puts it on the menu alongside Oxtail Bunny Chow from South Africa, an Idli & Shrimp dish inspired by South Indian and Indonesian traditions, and the Nasi Kandar Feast — a hearty Indo-Malay spread of rice, curries, and side dishes. The result is a restaurant that is less about Indian food and more about what Indian food *became* when Indian people moved.

## The Chef's Own Migration

Sampath relocated from Mumbai to the United States in 2013, building her culinary career through a series of television appearances that included winning both Chopped and Beat Bobby Flay on the Food Network. But her debut restaurant isn't a showcase for competition-circuit pyrotechnics. It is, she has said, an attempt to tell the story of South Asian food migration — the dishes that evolved when communities from India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and Nepal put down roots in Trinidad, Guyana, South Africa, Malaysia, and beyond.

Drāvida — named for the geographic region of South India, its people, and their family of languages — occupies a renovated century-old building at 211 1st Avenue. Spread across two floors, it pairs heritage architecture with contemporary design. Upstairs, a 20-seat speakeasy called Jam and Jaggery serves inventive cocktails: the Passionfruit Lassi, the Drāvida Highball, and the Orange Cream, all reframing South Asian flavours through a bar programme.

## The Overlooked Cuisines

What makes Drāvida conceptually ambitious is its focus on home-cooked dishes and regional cuisines that rarely make it onto restaurant menus — even in a city with as many Indian restaurants as New York.

South Africa's Bunny Chow, a hollowed-out loaf of bread filled with curry, was born in Durban's Indian community. It has never had a proper American restaurant champion. Trinidad's Doubles are a cornerstone of Caribbean-Indian identity but are largely invisible in Manhattan's Indian dining scene. The Nasi Kandar Feast traces the influence of Tamil Muslim traders on Malaysian cuisine, a culinary footnote most Americans have never encountered.

By placing these dishes alongside each other, Drāvida makes an implicit argument: that the Indian diaspora's food story is not a single narrative radiating outward from Delhi and Mumbai. It is a web of parallel migrations, each producing its own cuisine, its own comfort foods, its own debates about what counts as "authentic."

## A Growing Appetite for Diaspora Stories

Drāvida arrives at a moment when the American restaurant industry is more receptive to these stories than ever. Datassential data shows 49% of US consumers have dined at an Indian restaurant, while Technomic finds that 52% have tried Indian food and liked it. But the cuisine that drove those numbers — chicken tikka masala, butter chicken, naan — represents a narrow slice of a vastly complex culinary tradition.

The shift is visible in the kinds of Indian restaurants opening across the country this summer. In Phoenix, NADU — from Michelin-starred chef Sujan Sarkar — is built around regional diversity, with Kashmiri roganjosh sitting alongside Benne masala dosa and Kerala-style beef ularthiyathu. In the Hudson Valley, The 100 Food Journey cycles its entire menu every 100 days, each cycle devoted to a different region. Even The Kati Roll Company, opening its first New Jersey location in July, is built on a single regional speciality: the Kolkata street roll.

## What Diaspora Food Means to NRIs

For Indian Americans, Drāvida's menu raises a question that resonates beyond the table: what happens to your food when you leave? The dishes your grandparents cooked evolve. They absorb local ingredients, accommodate new climates, and eventually become something your family back in India might not recognise. Are they still Indian?

The Trinidadian answer is yes. The South African answer is yes. The Malaysian answer is yes. And Sampath's answer, served on plates in a century-old East Village building, is the most emphatic of all: not only are they still Indian, they are *the* Indian food story — the one about movement, adaptation, and survival.

Drāvida is located at 211 1st Avenue, Manhattan. Reservations are available online.
